newsitem.title: USA: Clinton pressures Senate to back weapons treaty.
newsitem.headline: Clinton pressures Senate to back weapons treaty.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton increased pressure on the Republican-led Senate on Friday to ratify a global chemical weapons treaty that supporters said was in doubt.

"The bottom line is this: Will the United States join a treaty we helped to shape? Or will we go from leading the fight against poison gas to joining the company of pariah nations this treaty seeks to isolate?" the president said.

Clinton used a hastily called news conference to lobby for Senate ratification next week of the Chemical Weapons Convention, which goes into force on April 29, with or without U.S. participation. The treaty, already ratified by more than 70 countries, bars development, production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons.

"America should stand with those who want to destroy chemical weapons, not with those who defy the international community. I urge every member of the Senate to support the convention when it comes to a vote next week," Clinton said.
The president took aim at four so-called "killer amendments" to the treaty that opponents have proposed to try to derail ratification.

If approved, they would raise the standards of verification against cheating to unachievable levels; link U.S. participation to Russian ratification of the pact; insist that Iraq and Libya join before America; and force renegotiating the treaty to fix other concerns Clinton said were already resolved.
"We should all understand what's at stake," Clinton said. "A vote for any of these killer amendments will prevent our participation in the treaty."

Treaty supporters in the Senate staged a news conference trying to build support for the treaty, the day after the Senate agreed to bring it to the floor for debate and a vote. A two-thirds majority -- 67 of the 100 senators -- is required for approval.

"We're six days away from an enormously important vote in the Senate and no one has a clue whether this treaty will be ratified," Sen. Byron Dorgan, a North Dakota Democat, told reporters. He said the vote, scheduled for Thursday, was "very much in doubt."
Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota told reporters the treaty had a 50-50 chance of passing.

Clinton denied that his decision to reorganize the State Department to include two agencies that had been independent was aimed at appeasing critics like Sen. Jesse Helms, a conservative North Carolina Republican, in hopes he would end his opposition to ratifying the treaty.

Helms had long sought the reorganization to cut the bureaucracy and spending. Under the plan approved by Clinton and Vice President Al Gore, the Arms Control and Disarmament Agency and the U.S. Information Agency will be placed under the jurisdiction of the State Department.
The Agency for International Development, which administers development aid and humanitarian assistance, will remain independent but its director will report to the secretary of state.
The announcement was made the day after Helms consented to let the treaty come to the Senate floor for a vote.
"I can tell you that there was no linkage between these two issues," Clinton insisted. "I do not expect Sen. Helms to vote for the Chemical Weapons Convention."
